title: Cross-Site Scripting
learning_outcomes: Explain what cross-site scripting contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: reflected xss.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. In this lesson, focus on reflected xss; then compare it with stored xss. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use cross-site scripting when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Security begins at trust boundaries. Validate data for the intended operation, encode output for its exact context, constrain file and network access, protect credentials, and apply authorization consistently. For cross-site scripting, begin with reflected xss. Also distinguish stored xss; html text and attribute contexts; javascript and url contexts. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: Reflected XSS
items.text: Treat the relevant value as untrusted, apply the defense at the correct boundary, and verify a deliberately invalid or hostile-looking input is rejected or encoded.

items.title: Stored XSS
items.text: Treat the relevant value as untrusted, apply the defense at the correct boundary, and verify a deliberately invalid or hostile-looking input is rejected or encoded.

items.title: HTML text and attribute contexts
items.text: State which values are accepted and what contract the declaration enforces; include a case that should be rejected or handled explicitly.

items.title: JavaScript and URL contexts
items.text: Know when to use javascript and url contexts, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: Context-appropriate escaping
items.text: Expect network failures and malformed responses; validate the response, set bounded timeouts, and make repeat delivery safe where needed.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Validate data at system boundaries and encode output for the target context; validation and escaping solve different problems.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for cross-site scripting from top to bottom. Start by identifying reflected xss, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

content.task: Create a second small example for cross-site scripting that demonstrates "reflected xss". Before running it, write down the expected result and one boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes a clear use of reflected xss.
The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.
At least one edge case is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input validation as output escaping.
common_mistakes.why: A value can be valid data and still be unsafe in an HTML or JavaScript output context.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate shape and business rules at input boundaries, then apply context-appropriate output encoding.

common_mistakes.why: A request can be sent without the original form or browser UI.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat all security-relevant validation and authorization on the server.

common_mistakes.problem: Returning internal error details to the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Stack traces and configuration values may expose sensitive information.
common_mistakes.fix: Log safe diagnostics server-side and return a generic, useful response.

summary: Cross-Site Scripting is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Validate data at system boundaries and encode output for the target context; validation and escaping solve different problems.
